explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, the song says he "…planted the finest vines." Not the okay ones, not the leftovers from the clearance rack. I know a thing or two about being picked up cheap, so a owner who goes straight for the best gets my respect. Everything he did for this hill was top shelf.

Youngest has a nice ring to it, but the verse never mentions age. It says he planted "…the finest vines." Notice the song is bragging about quality, not how old the vines were. That tells us this owner wasn't cutting corners.

Tallest is a fun guess, friend, but the verse says nothing about height. The song says he "…planted the finest vines." That's the word to hold onto. The owner is picking the best he can get, whatever size they come in.

That's it, baker. The verse says he "…dug out a winepress as well." A winepress is where grapes get crushed to make wine, so he's planning for a harvest. Watchtower, finest vines and a winepress: this owner thought of everything.

A well is a smart idea for a vineyard, but this song doesn't mention one. What the owner dug out was a winepress, the spot where grapes get pressed for their juice. Easy one to miss when you're picturing everything a vineyard could use. The song sticks to what he actually dug.

A storehouse sounds handy for all those grapes, friend, but it's not in this verse. The song says he "…dug out a winepress as well." Notice he dug it out, so it was carved into the ground. I think he was getting ready for the grapes, and the text shows us the winepress.

Right, baker. The verse says he waited for good grapes, "…but the fruit it produced was sour!" That exclamation point says a lot. After all that digging, planting and building, sour is not what anybody ordered.

Close, but there was fruit. The verse says "…the fruit it produced was sour!" So the vines did produce something. It just wasn't the good grapes he waited for, and I think that makes it sting even more.

The song never talks about the size of the harvest, friend. It says he waited for good grapes, "…but the fruit it produced was sour!" The problem is the taste, not the amount. Picture me pulling out a full tray, golden and gorgeous, and the first bite is pure salt. Nobody at that table is asking how many cookies there are, baker.

explanations.answer: Judge between him and his vineyard
explanations.explanation: Yep. The owner says, "…I exhort you to judge between Me and My vineyard." He's talking to the dwellers of Jerusalem and the men of Judah, and he's putting the question in their hands. It's like he sets the whole case in front of them and says, you tell me.

explanations.answer: Help him replant the whole vineyard
explanations.explanation: Replanting would be a big job, friend, but he never asks for helpers. What he asks is that they "…judge between Me and My vineyard." He wants their verdict. The song leaves the shovels out of it.

Nobody's making an offer here, baker. There's no sale in this song at all. The owner says to the people of Jerusalem and Judah, "…judge between Me and My vineyard." He's asking them to weigh in, not open their wallets.

True, baker. He asks, "What more could have been done for My vineyard than I have done for it?" It's a question with nothing left to add. He dug, cleared, planted, built and waited, and then he asks that question.

It's actually true, friend. The text has the owner ask, "What more could have been done for My vineyard than I have done for it?" He puts that question to the people of Jerusalem and Judah. Then he asks, "Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit?"

That's right. The owner says, "I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled." A wall is what keeps things out, so once it's down, the vineyard is open to whoever walks through. It's a heavy moment in the song, and I think it's meant to be.
Giving it away isn't what he says, baker. The line is, "I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled." So the vineyard doesn't get a new owner here. It gets walked all over.

There's no sale in this part, friend. The owner says, "I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled." He also says he'll take away its hedge, so the protection around the vineyard is gone. With the wall down, being walked over is what's coming, not being sold.

Not quite, baker, this one is false. The owner says, "I will make it a wasteland, neither pruned nor cultivated, and thorns and briers will grow up." That's no plan for a second try. The vineyard is left untended, and thorns and briers are what grow.

Correct, it's false. The owner says, "I will make it a wasteland, neither pruned nor cultivated, and thorns and briers will grow up." No more pruning and no more tending. The song says the opposite of a second try.
Close, but this is false, friend. The owner says, "I will command the clouds that rain shall not fall on it." So he's not sending extra rain. He's commanding that none fall on it.

Right, false. The owner says, "I will command the clouds that rain shall not fall on it." That's the last thing he lists, and it's the opposite of pouring rain. Wasteland, thorns and briers, and no rain to follow.
Yes, baker. Verse 7 says, "For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel…" That's the verse where the song tells us what the vineyard stands for. The vineyard belongs to Him.

Solomon is a fair guess, friend, but the song doesn't name him. It says, "…the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel…" The owner of this vineyard is the LORD of Hosts. Kings come and go, and this song points to Him.

Naboth was a man from Jezreel who owned a vineyard (1 Kings 21:1). That's a different story, baker. In this song, verse 7 says, "…the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel…" So the vineyard here is the LORD's.

That's it, baker. Verse 7 says, "…the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel…" And the men of Judah are called "…the plant of His delight." Once you know that, every part of the song about the vineyard hits closer to home.
Egypt isn't in this song, friend. Verse 7 says the vineyard "…is the house of Israel…" The song is about the LORD's own people. Good thing it doesn't send you off to a different country.

Persia doesn't show up here, baker. The verse says, "…the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel…" So the song is talking about Israel the whole way through. Keep your eyes on Israel and the men of Judah.
Yes, baker. The verse says, "He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed…" This is a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be. He wanted justice from the plant of His delight and saw bloodshed instead.

Idol worship isn't what this verse says, friend. It says, "He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed…" Notice how this lands on people hurting people, not just on something people bowed down to. I think that's why the next line is about a cry of distress: "for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress."

Laziness isn't in this verse, baker. The text says, "He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed…" Nobody here is accused of napping on the job. The next line says He looked for righteousness, "…but heard a cry of distress."
